newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heating oil ends higher on inventory drop.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heating oil ends higher on inventory drop.

text.p: NYMEX heating oil prices ended higher Wednesday on an unexpected draw in historically low distillate inventories, while crude oil ended lower as it was caught in a downdraft created by gasoline's slippage.
"Heating oil was definitely the leader, while crude and gasoline traded separately," said Jack McIntyre, market strategist with MCM Trade Watch.

November heating oil settled 1.22 cents higher at 71.98 cents a gallon. November crude settled nine cents lower at $24.05 a barrel, and November gasoline settled off 0.40 cent at 62.42 cents a gallon.
Heating oil hit a fresh post-Gulf War high of 73.15 cents mid-session, shattering the previous high of 72.80 made only last week.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) said Wednesday that for the week ended September 27, distillate stocks, which include heating oil, dropped 800,000 barrels. Traders were expecting a build of about two million barrels.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said heating oil stocks are 17.9 million barrels below a year ago. Most of the shortfall is in the northeastern United States, the world's largest market for heating oil.
Dealers said exports to Europe, where heating oil is also in tight supply, are draining U.S. supplies.

Meanwhile, traders said poor demand is fattening gasoline stocks. The API reported that gasoline inventories rose 2.27 million barrels, and the EIA data showed an even higher build of 4.2 million barrels.
Traders also attributed the build to high refinery runs, which are operating at a feverish 95.5 percent.

Gains in heating oil had been sharpened by a rumor of a fire at the Punta Cardon refinery of Venezuela's Maraven, a unit of state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), but a PDVSA spokesman denied the rumor, weakening oil prices generally.
"Once the Venezuelan story was denied, the market came off," said Prudential Securities trader Nauman Barakat.
The rumor may have been started by a fire drill which took place earlier Wednesday, the PDVSA spokesman said.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
